Apache people

Lipan Apache

Lipan Apache is a living people whose community histories cross Texas, northern Mexico, and neighboring regions. Lipan Apache accounts and historical scholarship describe multiple bands, settlements, and routes; present-day communities should not be collapsed into one historical movement or equated with every Apache community.

Still unfinished

This Texas-focused collection now contains fourteen substantive inspected works, including Tribe-hosted history and treaty records, a full scholarly place-name study, the text of a ratified multination treaty, federal correspondence about a small Lipan group at Fort Griffin, and local reporting on a contemporary Presidio historical-stewardship project. The numerical target is exceeded, but the collection remains unfinished: direct community-source depth and coverage of related Lipan communities remain uneven; treaty implementation and party-specific responses are unverified; two earlier treaty scans and two full theses/dissertations remain unread; and legal and chronology questions remain open. The 1876 federal report describes one group and government proposals, while the 2024 news report documents one local project through attributed interviews; neither should be generalized to all Lipan people. No community review is recorded.

Assessment recorded October 23, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • The 1838 and 1844 treaty scans linked by the Tribe were not readable in the available reader; do not treat the landing pages as inspected treaty text. The 1846 multination treaty was read, but it does not establish implementation or a uniform Lipan response.
  • The 2026 UTEP dissertation and 2016 UTRGV thesis were inspected only through repository abstracts; full texts returned automated HTTP 403 responses and remain unread and uncounted.
  • The TSHA article is an outside historical synthesis; its bibliography points to community historians, archival records and scholarship that require separate review.
  • The 1903/1904 difference for Lipan arrivals at the Mescalero community and the 1934/1936 reorganization dates need source-level resolution.
  • The Texas State Library and Archives map 01413 remains metadata-only; the image was not inspected and no map-to-profile association has been made.
  • The Webster place-name article is based primarily on one narrator’s 1938 account, includes some unidentified locations, and should not be used to draw a fixed homeland boundary or generalize beyond its own small sample.
  • Current legal status, enrollment, population, language use and relationships among Lipan communities in Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma and northern Mexico require further, carefully scoped research.
  • No community review or endorsement has been recorded.
  • The 1876 Fort Griffin report is a federal administrative compilation. Its statements concern one Lipan group and federal policy; underlying records, a Lipan-authored interpretation, and whether recommendations were implemented remain unverified.
  • The 2024 Marfa Public Radio report is a useful dated local case study, not a comprehensive history written by the Tribe; the audio was not played, and its accounts should remain attributed to the interviewees.
01

A living people and a present-day community

The Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas describes a united Lipan Apache community today while preserving the names and histories of distinct historical bands. Its account places families in Texas and across the border in northern Mexico and also describes later Lipan participation in the Mescalero Apache community. These records do not make every Lipan family’s history identical or make the Tribe interchangeable with other Apache governments.

Read the sources [1] Lipan Apache Tribe [3] Lipan Apache Tribe [10] Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association; Brandon Seale [11] Mescalero Apache Tribe

02

Place, movement, and regional history

The Tribe-hosted homeland essay and its community-contributed timeline describe relationships with the upper Brazos, Colorado, Concho, San Antonio, Rio Grande and northern Mexican communities across different periods. Brandon Seale’s Handbook of Texas account offers a broader scholarly narrative. Anthony K. Webster’s linguistic study examines place names in Augustina Zuazua’s 1938 narrative to Harry Hoijer; the article gives different totals in its main text and notes, leaves some locations unidentified, and cautions against broad conclusions from this small sample. These accounts offer historically situated evidence, not a surveyed boundary or proof that all places were occupied at the same time.

Read the sources [4] Lipan Apache Tribe; article by Nancy McGown Minor [3] Lipan Apache Tribe [10] Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association; Brandon Seale [17] Anthony K. Webster, Names: A Journal of Onomastics 55(2)

03

Diplomacy across Spanish, Mexican, and Texas governments

Community-authored histories discuss Lipan diplomacy with Mexican and Republic of Texas authorities, including the Bustamante agreement and the 1838 Treaty of Live Oak Point. The Tribe-reproduced 1846 Council Springs treaty is a multination U.S. instrument that names Lipan alongside other Native parties; its articles address U.S.-directed trade regulation, prisoners, legal arrangements, and other terms. The Indigenous Digital Archive/National Archives catalogue gives a March 8, 1847 ratification date, though its normalized named-nations field omits Lipan. This record does not establish implementation or a single Lipan response. The 1838 and 1844 treaty scans remain unread, so their terms are not independently summarized here.

Read the sources [5] Lipan Apache Tribe; article by Nancy McGown Minor [6] Lipan Apache Tribe; article by Nancy McGown Minor [10] Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association; Brandon Seale [12] Lipan Apache Tribe [13] Lipan Apache Tribe [18] United States commissioners and named Native parties; treaty text reproduced by the Lipan Apache Tribe [19] Indigenous Digital Archive Treaties Explorer / National Archives partnership

04

Displacement, borderlands, and community continuity

The Tribe-hosted account of nineteenth-century campaigns describes Lipan communities in Coahuila and cross-border military attacks; its language and interpretation are attributed to the author. The TSHA entry supplies a related scholarly synthesis and describes later Lipan communities in Texas and northern Mexico. Neither sparse government records nor movement into Mexico or another Apache community establish that Lipan people disappeared.

Read the sources [7] Lipan Apache Tribe; article by Nancy McGown Minor [10] Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association; Brandon Seale [3] Lipan Apache Tribe

05

Different paths during the reservation era

The Tribe-hosted reservation-era essay describes different Lipan groups moving to Mescalero, Tonkawa, Mexican, and Texas communities. The Mescalero Apache Tribe’s own history says Lipan survivors joined its community in about 1903; the Lipan Tribe-hosted essay dates one group’s joining to 1904. These accounts concern related but not necessarily identical events, and the one-year difference remains unresolved. A 2021 Fort Davis National Historic Site page says Lipan had no longer a “discernible presence” in their homeland after some families joined Mescalero. Later community and scholarly accounts document continuing Lipan communities and institutions, so the NPS phrase is not used here as evidence that Lipan people disappeared. Its stated 1936 Mescalero incorporation date also differs from the Mescalero Tribe’s 1934 date. A 1876 federal compilation adds a separate Fort Griffin strand: officials reported that a small Lipan group moved there from Fort Sill in 1874, and the 1875 Interior Department commissioner described intermarriage with Tonkawa people and considered several possible relocation arrangements. This is administrative correspondence, not a Lipan account; it does not show that the proposed consolidation or removal occurred and cannot stand for all Lipan groups.

Read the sources [8] Lipan Apache Tribe; article by Nancy McGown Minor [11] Mescalero Apache Tribe [2] National Park Service [10] Handbook of Texas Online / Texas State Historical Association; Brandon Seale [1] Lipan Apache Tribe [20] U.S. Government Publishing Office, Congressional Serial Set; digitized by the Law Library of Congress

06

Present-day institutions and public historical work

The Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas describes its Tribal Council and unified community, and it documents a 2021 transfer of a Presidio cemetery to the Tribe and a later collaboration around site protection and interpretation. A 2026 congressional bill proposing federal recognition was introduced and referred to committee; that proposed legislation is not an enacted law. This page makes no current population claim and does not substitute for the Tribe’s own legal or membership information. A 2024 local report follows the completion of a Presidio cemetery protection project, documenting participation by descendants and Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas leadership. It describes a historical-marker text drafted by an enrolled member in collaboration with the Texas Historical Commission and public historical interpretation developed for the site. These interviews document one dated local project and its participants, not all Lipan communities or a comprehensive account of Lipan history.

Read the sources [1] Lipan Apache Tribe [9] Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas [16] United States Congress / Government Publishing Office [21] Marfa Public Radio

07

Lipan people at Fort Griffin in federal records, 1874–1876

An eight-page 1876 congressional document reproduces federal and military correspondence about Lipan people at Fort Griffin alongside Tonkawa people. Officials report authorizing a small Lipan group to move from Fort Sill in 1874, ending regular ration issues in 1875, and seeking help for both communities. An Interior Department letter describes the Lipans as related to Tonkawa people by intermarriage and considers possible destinations, including Mescalero or Hot Springs agencies. This is a colonial administrative record: its labels, descriptions, and policy proposals reflect federal officials. It does not establish a general Lipan-Tonkawa political merger, prove any proposed move occurred, or represent every Lipan community.

Read the sources [20] U.S. Government Publishing Office, Congressional Serial Set; digitized by the Law Library of Congress

What needs further research

  • The 1838 and 1844 treaty scans linked by the Tribe were not readable in the available reader; do not treat the landing pages as inspected treaty text. The 1846 multination treaty was read, but its implementation and Lipan-specific response remain unverified.
  • The 2026 UTEP dissertation and 2016 UTRGV thesis were inspected only through repository abstracts; full texts returned automated HTTP 403 responses and remain unread and uncounted.
  • The TSHA article is an outside historical synthesis; its bibliography points to community historians, archival records and scholarship that require separate review.
  • The 1903/1904 difference for Lipan arrivals at the Mescalero community and the 1934/1936 reorganization dates need source-level resolution.
  • The Texas State Library and Archives map 01413 remains metadata-only; the image was not inspected and no map-to-profile association has been made.
  • The Webster place-name article is based primarily on one narrator’s 1938 account and includes unidentified locations; it cannot support a fixed homeland boundary or broad conclusions about all Lipan place-naming practices.
  • Current legal status, enrollment, population, language use and relationships among Lipan communities in Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma and northern Mexico require further, carefully scoped research.
  • No community review or endorsement has been recorded.

October 22, 2026 follow-up: the collection now has twelve substantive inspected works (ten previously counted, plus Webster’s 2007 article and the 1846 Council Springs treaty text), seven supporting records excluded from the count, and six cited sections. Reaching the numerical target does not complete the research or establish adequacy/community endorsement. Webster’s full article analyzes place names centered on Augustina Zuazua’s 1938 narrative. The article cautions that broad claims cannot be made from its small sample; the abstract/main discussion mention 22 names while a note mentions a twenty-third, and some places are unidentified. The Atlas uses it as attributed linguistic/ethnohistorical interpretation, not as a boundary source. The full six-page 1846 Council Springs treaty text was read. It is a multination instrument naming Lipan among other Native parties and was ratified in 1847 according to the Indigenous Digital Archive/National Archives catalogue. The catalogue’s normalized “Named Native nations” field omits Lipan despite its title and the treaty preamble; this indexing discrepancy is preserved. Treaty text is not evidence by itself of implementation, a uniform Lipan response, or a modern homeland boundary. The 2026 H.R. 10435 text and UTEP dissertation abstract were rechecked as supporting records only. Proposed legislative findings and a dissertation abstract are attributed positions, not independently corroborated findings; the full dissertation and the UTRGV thesis remain unread after automated HTTP 403 responses. The earlier Lipan source review remains valid for its original eight-source addition and other inspection limits. The current initial adequacy is Still unfinished because substantive gaps remain despite reaching twelve inspected works. No historical map was added or assigned.

Lipan Apache Placenames of Augustina Zuazua: Some Structural and Discursive Features ↗

A linguistic and ethnohistorical analysis centered on Augustina Zuazua’s 1938 narrative to Harry Hoijer. Webster examines how place names work in that account and cautions that a small sample from one narrator cannot support broad claims about all Lipan Apache naming practices. The article’s abstract and main text refer to 22 names, while a note identifies a twenty-third; several locations remain unidentified. These names are not a surveyed boundary or a statement of present-day territorial extent.

Inspection scope: The full 20-page article was read, including its discussion of the 1938 narrative, place-name forms and discourse, comparative analysis, conclusion and notes. The author explicitly limits generalization because the corpus is small and centered on one narrator. Some locations are unidentified; no new boundary geometry is inferred.

Tonkawa Indians at Fort Griffin, Texas — H. Ex. Doc. 44-102 ↗

The congressional document records federal officials’ accounts of a small Lipan group moving from Fort Sill to Fort Griffin in 1874, subsequent ration decisions affecting Tonkawa and Lipan people there, and proposed removal options. The 1875 Interior Department letter reports kinship through intermarriage and discusses a possible consolidation; it is an official’s account and recommendation, not a Lipan-authored history or evidence that the proposal was implemented. It must not be generalized to all Lipan people or treated as proof of incorporation into Mescalero Apache.

Inspection scope: Read the full searchable text of the eight-page public PDF, including its letters and reports dated 1872–1876. The OCR text was inspected; the page images, handwriting, signatures, and original correspondence files were not independently inspected. The authors write from federal and military administrative positions, not as Tonkawa or Lipan narrators. No reader access restriction was encountered.

In Presidio, the effort to preserve an Indigenous cemetery is finally complete ↗

Annie Rosenthal reports on the completion of a community-led protection and interpretation project at a Presidio cemetery. Interviewed descendants, an anthropologist, the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas vice-chairman, local conservation partners, and the project architect describe their different roles. The story reports that a descendant drafted historical-marker text in collaboration with the Texas Historical Commission and that the completed site includes public historical and cultural interpretation. Use it as a dated local case study of contemporary community stewardship, not as a complete account of the Tribe or of Lipan communities generally. The profile summarizes the public-history work and omits sensitive burial details.

Inspection scope: Read the complete visible article text (approximately six-minute audio story) and captions on October 23, 2026, paragraphs covering the 2024 completion of the Presidio cemetery protection project, local descendant participation, Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas leadership, and the collaboratively drafted historical-marker interpretation. The audio itself was not played and the article photographs were not used. This is local reporting based on attributed interviews, not a comprehensive Tribe-authored history; no access restriction interrupted reading.
